name: a01-secret-order
title: Remediate a committed secret in four steps
spec: Four boxes in a row from left to right, each with a numbered circle (1 to 4) and one outline icon. Box 1, orange outline (the most important step), key icon, title 'Revoke and rotate', text 'Revoke and rotate the credential right away, because a copy may already exist'. Box 2, lock icon, title 'Remove the secret from the current tree', text 'Replace it with a reference to a secret manager'. Box 3, clock-with-history or branch icon, title 'Purge history (optional)', text 'git filter-repo --path secrets.yml --invert-paths', then 'Force-push, and ask collaborators to re-clone'. Box 4, shield icon, title 'Prevent the next leak', text 'Add gitleaks or push protection, and .gitignore entries'. Arrows point from box 1 to 2, 2 to 3, and 3 to 4. Under box 1, a short note: 'Rotation comes first. You cannot take back a copy that someone already made.' Under box 3, a note: 'Rewriting history is slow and never complete.'
alt: Four ordered steps for a leaked secret: rotate it first, remove it from the tree, optionally purge history, then prevent a repeat.
cap: When a secret is committed, rotate it first, then remove it, purge history if needed, and prevent the next leak.

name: a01-onto
title: rebase --onto moves only the feature-B commits
spec: Top to bottom, two parts. Top row, a horizontal line labelled 'main' with a single box labelled 'squash commit' on it (the one new commit that the squash merge of feature-A created). Below it, a second horizontal line labelled 'feature-A' with two grey boxes 'A1' and 'A2' (the old commits, which no longer match anything on main). Branching off A2 is a third line labelled 'feature-B' with two green boxes 'B1' and 'B2'. Step 1 (number circle), an arrow labelled 'git rebase --onto main feature-A feature-B' pointing down to the final state. Final state row, a line labelled 'main' with the squash commit followed by two green boxes 'B1' and 'B2' now sitting on top of it. The grey A1 and A2 boxes are not copied across. Orange note on the grey boxes: 'Without --onto, the old feature-A commits would be replayed too.'
alt: The rebase --onto command replays only the feature-B commits onto main after feature-A was squash-merged.
cap: The rebase onto command moves only the feature-B commits onto main after feature-A was squash-merged.

name: a01-reflog-rescue
title: The reflog rescues a commit lost by reset --hard
spec: Three steps left to right, each with a numbered circle. Step 1, icon of a warning triangle or reset arrow, box text 'git reset --hard' with note 'The commit is still in the object store until cleanup'. Step 2, clock or ship's-log icon, box text 'git reflog' showing one line 'HEAD@{1}: commit: ...' with the line before the mistake highlighted. Step 3, branch icon, box text 'git branch rescue HEAD@{1}' with note 'The lost commit is back on a new branch'. Arrows connect 1 to 2 to 3. Orange highlight on the HEAD@{1} line. Under the row, a small note panel: 'The reflog is local only, so it does not survive a fresh clone.'
alt: A commit lost by reset --hard is found in the reflog as HEAD@{1} and restored onto a new branch.
cap: After a reset --hard, git reflog shows the lost commit, and a new branch can point back to it.

name: a02-wisb-replace
title: A merge keeps the stale neighbor, a replace matches the file
spec: Two side-by-side panels with a green heading each. Left panel, heading 'merge': a box labelled 'What It Should Be (WISB)' listing two neighbor stanzas, 'neighbor A' and 'neighbor B' (the neighbor C was deleted from Git). Below it, a box labelled 'What It Really Is (WIRI) on the router' listing A, B and a grey leftover 'neighbor C'. Note under the left panel: 'A merge only adds and updates lines, so the deleted neighbor stays on the router.' Right panel, heading 'replace': the same WISB box with A and B, with the monospace line '<bgp operation="replace">' above the arrow. Below it, the WIRI box lists only A and B, and neighbor C is gone. Note under the right panel: 'A replace makes the section match the file exactly.' An orange arrow from the grey leftover C on the left panel to the replace operation on the right panel, labelled 'removed'. Bottom line in a green bar, plain text: 'WISB equals WIRI'.
anchor: ### Foundations from *Network Programmability and Automation* (Ch. 13) and *Ansible: Up and Running* (Ch. 22)
alt: A merge leaves a deleted BGP neighbor on the router, while a replace operation removes it so the device matches the file.
cap: A merge leaves a deleted BGP neighbor on the router, but a replace operation makes the device match the file.

name: a02-oidc-exchange
title: A CI job swaps a short-lived token for cloud credentials
spec: Left to right, a chain of four boxes with arrows. Box 1 'CI runner', window icon, text 'One plan job starts'. Box 2 'CI provider', badge icon, text 'Mints a short-lived signed token with claims: repository and branch'. Box 3 'Cloud', shield icon, text 'Checks the signature and the claims against the rule'. Box 4 'Temporary credentials', key icon, text 'Expire when the job ends'. Arrow 1 to 2 labelled 'request token (id-token: write)'. Arrow 2 to 3 labelled 'send token'. Arrow 3 to 4 labelled 'if the claims match'. Below the chain, two small role cards side by side: 'tf-plan role (read-only)' with note 'pull request, never a fork', and 'tf-apply role (write)' with note 'protected branch and environment only'. Orange highlight on the 'tf-apply role' card with note 'A feature branch can never reach this role'. A grey note: 'No cloud key is stored in the repository.'
anchor: ## 5. Authentication: OIDC instead of stored keys
alt: A CI job exchanges a short-lived OIDC token for temporary cloud credentials, with separate plan and apply roles.
cap: A CI job trades a short-lived OIDC token for temporary cloud credentials, and only protected branches reach the apply role.

name: a02-drift-classes
title: Auto-heal stateless resources, alert on stateful ones
spec: Top, a single box 'Nightly drift check' with a clock icon, text 'terraform plan -detailed-exitcode'. Three exit-code boxes beneath it in a row with a number on each: '0' labelled 'no drift', '1' labelled 'error', '2' labelled 'drift detected'. From box '2' an arrow goes down into two columns. Left column, green panel, heading 'Auto-heal', gear icon, examples 'Kubernetes Deployments', 'ConfigMaps', 'host config files', note 'Reverting holds no data'. Right column, grey-green panel with orange outline, heading 'Alert only', lock icon, examples 'databases', 'storage buckets', 'VPCs', 'stateful GPU instances', note 'A revert could delete data, so never auto-apply'. Below the right column, a note: 'Post the plan diff to chat or a ticket.' Caption row at the bottom: 'Ask what the revert would do on its worst day.'
alt: A nightly drift check exits with code 2 on drift, then stateless resources auto-heal while stateful resources only raise an alert.
cap: A nightly drift check auto-heals stateless resources and only alerts on stateful ones, because a revert there could destroy data.

name: a03-push-pull
title: Push sends work out, pull lets each machine ask for it
spec: Two side-by-side panels, each with a green heading. Left panel, heading 'Push (Ansible)': one box 'Control node' at the top with a gear icon, and a row of three target boxes 'web1', 'web2', 'web3' beneath it (or GPU nodes). Solid arrows from the control node down to each target, labelled 'SSH: sends the task'. Note under the panel: 'No agent is installed on the targets. The control node decides when work happens.' Right panel, heading 'Pull (agent-based)': a server box 'Central server' at the top, and the same three target boxes beneath, each with a small 'agent' badge. Arrows point UP from each target to the server, labelled 'asks for work'. Note under the panel: 'Each machine decides when to ask. An agent runs on every machine.' Orange outline on the Push panel's control node, as the Ansible approach used in this chapter. Small caption at the bottom: 'Puppet, Chef and Salt pull. Ansible pushes.'
alt: Ansible pushes tasks from the control node over SSH with no agent, while pull tools have each machine ask a server for work.
cap: Ansible pushes tasks from a control node over SSH without an agent, while pull tools have each machine ask a server for work.

name: a03-split-tools
title: Terraform builds the machines, Ansible configures them
spec: A left-to-right chain of three boxes with arrows between them, each with a numbered circle. Box 1, cloud icon, title 'Terraform', text 'Builds a new pool of GPU VMs with the right network and disks'. Box 2, power-button icon, title 'cloud-init', text 'Handles the first boot, with a user and an SSH key'. Box 3, gear icon, title 'Ansible', text 'Installs the driver, sets the kernel parameters and starts the monitoring agent'. Arrow 1 to 2 labelled 'machines exist'. Arrow 2 to 3 labelled 'machines can be reached over SSH'. Above the chain, a grey banner: 'Each tool does one part of the job.' Under box 3, an orange note: 'Ansible decides what runs on the machines.' No other items.
alt: Terraform creates the GPU VMs, cloud-init handles the first boot, and Ansible configures the driver, kernel and monitoring agent.
cap: Terraform creates the machines, cloud-init handles the first boot, and Ansible decides what runs on them.

name: a03-linear-wait
title: The linear strategy makes every host wait at each task
spec: A timeline with three horizontal lanes labelled 'gpu01', 'gpu02' and 'gpu03', and time running left to right. Each lane has task boxes in order. Task 1 box in all three lanes, green, labelled 'ok'. Task 2 box: in gpu01 and gpu03 green 'ok'; in gpu02 a red-outline box 'failed'. A dashed vertical barrier after task 2 across all lanes, labelled 'linear: wait until every host finishes this task'. After the barrier, gpu02's lane shows a grey box 'dropped from later tasks' with a number '1'-step number circle on the barrier. Task 3 boxes appear only in gpu01 and gpu03, green, labelled 'ok'. The recap label at the far right of gpu02 lane: 'failed in the recap'. Orange highlight on the 'failed' box in gpu02. Caption under the timeline: 'One slow or failing host can hold up the whole run.'
alt: Under the linear strategy, a host that fails one task is dropped from later tasks while the other hosts wait at the next barrier.
cap: Under the linear strategy, a host that fails is dropped from later tasks while the other hosts wait at each barrier.

name: a04-yaml-coercion
title: Unquoted values change type, quoted values stay text
spec: A two-column table-style figure. Left column, heading 'You write (unquoted)', with monospace entries stacked vertically, each in a small box: 'NO', '1.10', '010', '22:30', '0644', '~'. Middle column, arrows labelled 'parser reads', each pointing right. Right column, heading 'The parser stores', with the matching results in boxes: 'NO' becomes 'false' (orange, the most important item, with the note 'the Norway problem'), '1.10' becomes '1.1', '010' becomes '8', '22:30' becomes a number, '0644' becomes '420', '~' becomes 'null'. Bottom band, green panel, heading 'Fix: quote it', with monospace examples 'country: "NO"' and 'mode: "0644"', and the note 'A quoted value is never reinterpreted.' Use a small outline icon of a magnifier or tag beside the heading. Keep text in the boxes short.
alt: Unquoted YAML values such as NO, 1.10, 010 and 0644 are converted to other types by the parser, while quoted values stay text.
cap: Unquoted YAML values such as NO and 0644 are converted to other types, so quoting them keeps them as text.

name: a04-anchor-merge
title: A merge key copies defaults, and a local key overrides them
spec: Top, a box labelled 'defaults (anchor: node_defaults)' listing three entries: 'gpus: 8', 'os: ubuntu-22.04', 'tags: [h100]'. A dashed arrow from the box to two node boxes below it, arrows labelled '<<: *node_defaults' (merge key). Left node box 'gpu01' shows the copied values 'gpus: 8', 'os', 'tags' with a green check. Right node box 'gpu02' shows the copied 'os' and 'tags', and a local line 'gpus: 4' in orange highlight, labelled 'override wins, local key comes after the merge'. Small note under gpu02: 'The other keys still come from the defaults.' Number circles 1 and 2 on the two arrows to show the order the parser reads them: defaults first, then each node.
alt: A YAML anchor holds shared defaults, a merge key copies them into each node, and a local key such as gpus 4 overrides the copied value.
cap: A YAML merge key copies shared defaults into each node, and a local key overrides the copied value.

name: a04-validate-install
title: Render on the control node, validate, then install
spec: A left-to-right flow of four boxes with arrows, each with a numbered circle. Box 1, window icon, title 'Control node', text 'Renders the .j2 template with the variables'. Box 2, gear icon, title 'Validate', text 'visudo -cf %s runs against the rendered temporary file'. Box 3, shield or lock icon, title 'Install', text 'Copies the finished file to the target'. Arrow 1 to 2 labelled 'rendered copy'. Arrow 2 to 3 labelled 'check passes'. From box 2 a second arrow goes down to a grey box 'Fails: the task aborts and the old file stays in place', labelled 'check fails'. Orange outline on the Validate box. Under the chain, a green panel with the note 'Jinja2 runs on the control node, so the target only receives plain text.' Monospace label for the command 'visudo -cf %s'.
alt: Ansible renders a template on the control node, runs the validate command on the rendered copy, and installs it only if the check passes.
cap: Ansible renders a template on the control node, validates the copy, and installs it only if the check passes.

name: a05-vagrant-collapse
title: Three hosts on one address collapse into one entry
spec: Two panels side by side with green headings. Left panel, heading 'Without aliases': three stacked input lines in monospace, '127.0.0.1:2222', '127.0.0.1:2200', '127.0.0.1:2201', each with an arrow pointing down into a single box labelled '127.0.0.1' (the inventory key). Below that box, one result box labelled 'one entry left' with an orange outline. A small note: 'Each line overwrites the same entry.' Right panel, heading 'With aliases': three boxes stacked, labelled 'vagrant1 ansible_port=2222', 'vagrant2 ansible_port=2200', 'vagrant3 ansible_port=2201', each with its own arrow to the same address label 'ansible_host=127.0.0.1' shown once in a group bracket labelled '[vagrant:vars]'. Result: three separate host boxes, labelled 'three hosts'. Green check mark on the result. Bottom caption: 'Give each machine its own logical name.'
anchor: ### Special groups, names and connection variables
alt: Three Vagrant entries that share 127.0.0.1 collapse into one host, and aliases with their own ports keep all three.
cap: Listing three Vagrant VMs by address alone collapses them into one host, so each machine needs its own alias.

name: a05-pattern-venn
title: Host patterns: union, intersection and exclusion
spec: Three overlapping circles drawn as a Venn diagram, labelled 'gpu' (large circle, left), 'login' (circle, right) and 'rack_r01' (circle, bottom). Use three light green fills with transparency. Below the diagram, a row of three example boxes, each with a monospace pattern and a one-line meaning: 'gpu:login' with the note 'Union: either group'; 'gpu:&rack_r01' with the note 'Intersection: both groups'; 'gpu:!gpu_a100' with the note 'Exclusion: the group without that one'. Highlight the overlap region of gpu and rack_r01 in orange with the label 'gpu:&rack_r01'. Icons: a small outline server icon beside 'gpu', a login-screen icon beside 'login', a rack icon beside 'rack_r01'. Caption: 'A host pattern is a filter on the inventory.'
alt: Venn diagram showing union, intersection and exclusion for host patterns over gpu, login and rack groups.
cap: Host patterns combine groups with union, intersection and exclusion, so you can pick an exact slice of the fleet.

name: a05-dynamic-flow
title: A plugin asks the cloud for the current hosts at run time
spec: Left to right, a chain of four boxes with arrows, each with a numbered circle. Box 1, document icon, title 'Plugin config file', monospace text 'plugin: google.cloud.gcp_compute' with a note 'File name ends with the required suffix'. Box 2, cloud icon, title 'Cloud API', text 'filters: labels.env = prod and status = RUNNING, so only matching instances come back'. Box 3, gear icon, title 'Build the groups and variables', two sub-lines: 'keyed_groups: role_gpu, role_login' and 'compose: ansible_host from networkInterfaces'. Box 4, list icon, title 'Inventory', text 'Current hosts, every time the command runs'. Arrow 1 to 2 labelled 'query at run time'. Arrow 2 to 3 labelled 'returned attributes'. Arrow 3 to 4 labelled 'groups and hosts'. Under box 4, a small orange note: 'Static files go stale. This list is read fresh on each run.' Under box 2, a grey note: 'cache: true keeps responses on disk.'
alt: A dynamic inventory plugin reads its config, queries the cloud API with filters, builds groups, and returns the current host list.
cap: A dynamic inventory plugin asks the cloud for the current hosts on each run, so the list never goes stale.

name: a05-hash-replace
title: A host dictionary replaces the group dictionary, combine keeps both
spec: Three columns, each with a heading. Column 1, 'Group dictionary (group_vars)': a box listing three keys 'key 1', 'key 2', 'key 3'. Column 2, 'Host override (host_vars)': a shorter box with only 'key 1' (note 'one key'). Column 3 splits into two rows. Top row, heading 'Default: replace', an arrow from the override box, result box showing only 'key 1', with keys 2 and 3 greyed out and crossed through, labelled 'keys 2 and 3 disappear'. Bottom row, heading 'combine(recursive=True)', result box showing 'key 1', 'key 2', 'key 3', with a green check, labelled 'keys are kept'. Orange outline on the 'replace' result. Monospace line under the bottom row: '{{ base_cfg | combine(env_cfg, recursive=True) }}'. Caption: 'Dictionaries replace across layers, so merge them on purpose.'
alt: A host dictionary replaces the whole group dictionary and drops its other keys, while the combine filter keeps all keys.
cap: A host dictionary replaces the group dictionary by default, so the combine filter is needed to keep the other keys.

name: a06-serial-gate
title: Serial batches grow, and a failure gate stops the rollout
spec: A left-to-right chain of three batch boxes with arrows between them, each with a numbered circle. Batch 1, title 'Canary', text 'serial: 1, one host runs the whole play'. Batch 2, title 'Next batch', text '10% of the group'. Batch 3, title 'The rest', text '25% for the remaining hosts'. Between each pair of batches, a diamond decision shape with the label 'Failures within max_fail_percentage: 5?'. A 'yes' arrow continues to the next batch. A 'no' arrow drops down to an orange box 'Play aborted; no later batch starts'. Icons: a single-host icon for the canary, a stack icon for the 10% batch, a server rack icon for the rest. Small note under the chain: 'serial: [1, "10%", "25%"]'. Caption under the orange box: 'A bad canary stops the rollout before it reaches the fleet.'
alt: Serial batches run a one-host canary, then 10 percent, then 25 percent, and a failure above the threshold aborts the play.
cap: Serial batches start with one canary host, grow in steps, and stop the play when failures pass the threshold.

name: a06-idempotent-runs
title: A second run must report changed=0
spec: Two horizontal rows, each showing two run boxes side by side with arrows. Row 1, heading 'Idempotent task', icon of a light switch: Run 1 box, green, text 'changed=2 (the work is done)'. Arrow labelled 'run again'. Run 2 box, green, text 'changed=0 (already correct)'. Green check mark at the end. Row 2, heading 'Timestamp in the template', clock icon: Run 1 box, amber-grey, text 'changed=1 (new timestamp written)'. Arrow labelled 'run again'. Run 2 box, orange outline, text 'changed=1 again, and the handler restarts the service'. Under row 2, a note: 'The rendered file differs on every run.' Under row 1, a note: 'A second run that changes things again means something is not idempotent.' Caption at the bottom: 'Run the playbook twice and read the second recap.'
alt: An idempotent task reports changed=0 on the second run, while a rendered timestamp makes every run report a change.
cap: An idempotent playbook reports changed=0 on its second run, while a timestamp in a template changes every run.

name: a06-check-scope
title: What --check previews and what it skips
spec: Two large panels side by side. Left panel, green heading 'Simulated by declarative modules': a list of five module boxes in monospace, 'package', 'file', 'template', 'service', 'sysctl', each with a small check-mark icon. Note under the list: '--check reports what would change, and --diff shows the content change.' Right panel, grey heading 'Skipped under --check': three module boxes in monospace, 'command', 'shell', 'raw', each with a dashed outline and a skip icon. Note under the list: 'Runs only with creates or removes, or with check_mode: false.' Below both panels, a full-width orange note: 'A later task that needs an earlier change judges a change that never happened.' A small green bar at the bottom: 'A clean check run is not proof that the change is safe.' Use an outline icon of a clipboard or magnifier beside the title.
alt: Check mode simulates declarative modules and skips command, shell and raw tasks unless they have a guard or check_mode false.
cap: Check mode simulates declarative modules, but it skips command, shell and raw tasks unless they have a guard.

name: a07-register-set-fact
title: register keeps the raw output, set_fact keeps the clean value
spec: A left-to-right row of four boxes, each with a green number circle (1 to 4) above it, joined by orthogonal arrows. Box 1, titled Run the command, shows the monospace text nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version --format=csv,noheader and the note Ansible runs it on the host. Arrow 1 is labelled register: drv. Box 2, titled Raw result in drv, lists the fields rc, stdout, stdout_lines, stderr, changed, failed, start, end, delta and cmd inside a light green panel, with the note the whole dictionary. Arrow 2 is labelled set_fact. Box 3, titled Clean value in current_driver, shows the monospace text drv.stdout_lines[0] | trim. Arrow 3 leads to Box 4, titled debug var: drv, which prints the whole structure so you can check each piece. Orange highlight on Box 3, the cleaned value that later tasks read. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Keep the raw output in register and the cleaned value in set_fact, so each variable does one job.
alt: A command's output is registered as a raw dictionary, set_fact trims the first line into a clean value, and debug shows the whole structure.
cap: The register step keeps the whole raw result, and set_fact turns one field of it into the clean value later tasks read.

name: a07-limit-hostvars
title: Why --limit breaks cross-host templates
spec: Two side-by-side panels with the same three-row picture each: a playbook box at the top, and below it a row of host boxes. Left panel titled Full run, with the note the play covers the whole cluster. Its host boxes are lb01, web1..3 and gpu001..032, all marked with a green tick labelled facts gathered. Below them a box labelled hostvars is complete, then an arrow down to a box labelled template writes every backend address. Right panel titled Run with --limit lb01, showing the command ansible-playbook site.yml --limit lb01 in monospace. Only the lb01 box is marked facts gathered; web1..3 and gpu001..032 are grey and marked not gathered. An arrow goes down to a box labelled hostvars for web1..3 or gpu001..032 is empty or undefined. From there an orange arrow leads to an outcome box labelled the template fails, or writes blank addresses. Below both panels, a green fix bar lists two boxes: first, a monospace play block with the lines - hosts: cluster, gather_facts: true, tasks: [], tags: [always]; second, the word cache, as in fact caching. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Before a limited run that templates across hosts, gather facts for the whole group.
alt: A limited run gathers facts only for one host, so hostvars for the other hosts is empty and the template fails or writes blank addresses.
cap: Running with --limit gathers facts for only one host, so a template that reads other hosts gets empty values.

name: a07-lookup-control-node
title: Lookups run on the control node, module results come from the target
spec: Three vertical zones side by side with a central task box. Left zone, a container titled Control node, with the note where you type ansible-playbook. Inside it, four small stacked boxes in monospace labelled lookup('file'), lookup('url'), lookup('env') and community.hashi_vault.hashi_vault, with the note lookups run here, when the template is rendered. A lane arrow from the Control node container points right into the centre box labelled Task uses the value. Right zone, a container titled Target host, with the note the machine being configured. Inside it a box labelled Module such as ansible.builtin.setup, drawn with a gear icon. An arrow from the Target host to the centre box is labelled register. Orange highlight on the Control node container and its arrow, with the note lookups never run on the targets. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: For data from a target, use a module and register instead, because a module runs on the host it describes.
alt: Lookups read data on the control node, while a module reads data on the target and returns it with register.
cap: Lookups fetch values on the control node when a template is rendered, while data from a target comes back through a module and register.

name: a07-extract-pipeline
title: map extract turns a group of hosts into a list of addresses
spec: A left-to-right assembly line of boxes with orthogonal arrows. Box 1 at the far left is a list titled gpu_nodes, drawn as stacked rows showing gpu001, gpu002 and an ellipsis. A hostvars cylinder sits above the first station, labelled hostvars, with a small note per row reading ansible_host. Station 1 is a box labelled map('extract', hostvars, 'ansible_host') with a green number circle 1 above it, with the note for each name, look up that host's ansible_host inside hostvars. Arrow to Station 2, a box labelled list with a green number circle 2 above it. Arrow to the final box at the far right titled Result, a plain list of addresses, drawn as stacked rows labelled 10.1.10.1 and 10.1.10.2 with an ellipsis. The Result box is highlighted in orange as the value ready for the next filter. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: The extract filter does the most work here, because it pulls one hostvar from many hosts at once.
alt: The map extract filter looks up ansible_host for each host name in hostvars, and the list filter returns a plain list of addresses.
cap: The map extract filter pulls one host variable for each name in a group, and the list filter turns the result into a plain list of addresses.

name: a08-handler-lost
title: A handler lost after a failure, and why Run 2 does not restart
spec: Two horizontal lanes stacked vertically, each with a bold lane title on the left. Top lane titled Run 1. Along it, three boxes left to right with green number circles 1, 2 and 3. Box 1: monospace template: dest=/etc/default/dcgm-exporter, with the note the file changes and the task reports changed. Arrow labelled notify to Box 2: queued handler Restart dcgm-exporter, with the note not yet run. Arrow labelled Task 2 to Box 3: a box labelled Task 2 fails on gpu01 with the note the handler is skipped and dcgm-exporter keeps the old config in memory. Box 3 is highlighted in orange. Bottom lane titled Run 2. Two boxes: Box A monospace template: dest=/etc/default/dcgm-exporter, with the note the file on disk already matches, so the task reports ok. Arrow labelled no notify to Box B, a box labelled no restart. Below both lanes, a light green panel titled Three fixes, with three stacked items: force_handlers: true on the play; meta: flush_handlers right after the critical config tasks; an idempotent task that checks the service uptime against the config file mtime. No takeaway bar.
alt: A changed config task queues a restart, a later task fails and the handler is skipped, and the second run reports ok so no restart happens.
cap: A handler can be lost when a later task fails in the same run, because the next run sees an unchanged file and never notifies it.

name: a08-import-include
title: import_tasks is read at parse time, include_tasks at run time
spec: A horizontal timeline across the top with two marked points: left point labelled Parse time, the playbook is read; right point labelled Run time, each task is reached in order. Below the timeline two side-by-side panels. Left panel titled import_tasks / import_role / import_playbook, marked with a lock or fixed-structure icon, with a note Static, at parse time. Inside it three bullet rows: visible to --list-tasks, --tags and --start-at-task; when is applied to every imported task; loop is not supported. Right panel titled include_tasks / include_role, marked with a gear or dynamic icon, with a note Dynamic, at runtime when reached. Inside it three rows: included tasks are not listed by --list-tasks; loop is supported, one include per item; the filename can use facts, shown in monospace as ansible_facts['os_family'] .yml. Under the panels, a decision box with the question: Can the file name or its existence change based on something the run discovers? Arrow labelled yes to a box labelled include. Arrow labelled no to a box labelled import, drawn in orange as the default choice. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Choose an import by default, and switch to an include only when runtime data forces your hand.
alt: Imports are read when the playbook is parsed and includes are read when the run reaches them, so a file name that depends on runtime facts needs an include.
cap: An import is fixed when the playbook is read, while an include is decided when the run reaches it, so the choice depends on whether the file name can change at runtime.

name: a08-serial-batches
title: serial batches grow from one canary node
spec: A horizontal row of three batch columns, left to right, each with a bold title and a green number circle: Batch 1, Batch 2 and Batch 3. Above the columns a monospace line: serial: [1, "10%", "25%"]. Each batch column holds a grid of small square icons, one square per host, drawn as server or chip icons in green outline. Batch 1 holds one square labelled as the canary, a single node, with the note first node is a test. Batch 2 holds squares covering a slice labelled 10%. Batch 3 holds a larger slice labelled 25%. Arrows between the columns are orthogonal and labelled in order. Below the columns, a light green panel with two rows: max_fail_percentage: 5 with the note stops the line when failures pass the limit; any_errors_fatal: false with the note a failure stays with its own host. Orange highlight on Batch 1, the one-node canary. A small note: the serial list grows in steps. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: The first node is a test, and only after that does the play work through larger slices of the fleet.
alt: The serial list runs a one-node canary first, then 10 percent and 25 percent slices, with a failure limit of 5 percent.
cap: The serial list starts with a single-node canary and then works through larger slices of the fleet, with a failure limit that stops the run.

name: a09-site-order
title: site.yml imports the tiers in dependency order
spec: A top-to-bottom or left-to-right chain of five boxes, joined by orthogonal arrows, each box with a green number circle (1 to 5) for the import order. Box 1: baseline.yml with a small tag label baseline and the note OS baseline on every host. Box 2: database.yml with tag label db and the note PostgreSQL on the db group. Box 3: app.yml with tag label app and the note application on the app group. Box 4: web.yml with tag label web and the note nginx reverse proxy. Box 5: verify.yml with tag label verify and the note end-to-end verification. Above the chain, a monospace file card titled playbooks/site.yml listing the five import_playbook lines in order. Beside the arrows, two small notes: --tags db runs only the tagged tier, and -l app limits the run to one host group, both in monospace. Box 3 and Box 4 are linked by a note the app must answer before the proxy sends it traffic. Orange highlight on the arrow from Box 2 to Box 3, labelled the database must exist before the app tries to connect. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: The database must exist before the app tries to connect, and the app must answer before the proxy sends it traffic.
alt: The site playbook imports baseline, database, app, web and verify in that order so each tier is ready before the next one depends on it.
cap: The site playbook imports five tier playbooks in dependency order, so each tier is ready before the next one depends on it.

name: a09-release-switch
title: Release directories and the atomic current symlink switch
spec: Left panel: a folder tree drawn with folder icons, titled /opt/fleetapp/. Inside it: releases/ containing two sub-folders, v1.4.1 with the note previous, which holds src/ and venv/, and v1.4.2 with the note new; shared/ with the note persistent data and config shared across releases; and a link icon labelled current pointing to releases/v1.4.2. Middle: a large orthogonal arrow from the new release folder to the current link, labelled switch current in one step. Right panel: a rollback box with the monospace command ansible-playbook playbooks/app.yml -e app_version=v1.4.1, and an arrow from it back to current labelled point it back to releases/v1.4.1, then restart the service. Orange highlight on the current link, the one pointer the service reads. A small note: app_keep_releases: 5 keeps the newest five releases; the release pruning command is shown in monospace. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Rolling back is the same flip in reverse, and the old folder is still there to go back to.
anchor: ## 5. The application play: release directories and an atomic switch
alt: Each release lives in its own folder, a current symlink points at the live one, and rollback repoints it to the previous folder.
cap: Each release gets its own folder and a current symlink points at the live one, so switching or rolling back is a single pointer change.

name: a09-verify-paths
title: Verification checks the path a user takes, then each app node
spec: A left-to-right flow of three numbered steps with green number circles 1, 2 and 3. A left column box titled verify.yml, drawn with a shield or check icon. Step 1 box: HTTPS endpoint answers, with the monospace line https://{{ nginx_server_name }}/readyz and the note the path a user takes, delegated to localhost. An arrow from Step 1 leads into a small nginx box, drawn with a router icon, labelled nginx, which leads to a Step 2 box. Step 2 box: Version served matches what we deployed, with the monospace check app_version and the note the assert compares the served version with the pinned one. Arrow from Step 2 to a Step 3 box: Every app node reports ready (direct), with the monospace line http://{{ hostvars[item]['ansible_host'] }}:{{ app_port }}/readyz, drawn as a fan-out to two app node boxes labelled app01 and app02, each with the note asked directly. Orange highlight on the Step 3 fan-out, labelled a single broken host is found even when nginx would have routed around it. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Modules verify state, while uri and assert verify behaviour, and you need both.
alt: The verification play calls the HTTPS readiness URL through nginx, checks the served version, then asks each app node directly.
cap: The verification play tests the public HTTPS path first, checks the served version, and then asks each app node directly.

name: a10-module-by-hand
title: Running a module by hand on the target
spec: A left-to-right sequence of five boxes joined by orthogonal arrows, each with a green number circle (1 to 5). Box 1 on the left, drawn with a laptop icon and titled Control node: the monospace command ANSIBLE_KEEP_REMOTE_FILES=1 ansible gpu001 -m ansible.builtin.copy -vvv. Arrow to Box 2, drawn with a server icon and titled gpu001 target: a box holding AnsiballZ_copy.py, with the note the wrapper stays on disk, and the monospace remote path /home/automation/.ansible/tmp/ansible-tmp-.../AnsiballZ_copy.py shown in the output. Arrow labelled ssh gpu001 to Box 3: monospace cd /home/automation/.ansible/tmp/ansible-tmp-*/. Arrow to Box 4: monospace python3 AnsiballZ_copy.py explode, with the note unpacks the module and its arguments into ./debug_dir. Arrow to Box 5: monospace python3 AnsiballZ_copy.py execute, with the note runs the module, where you can add a print or start pdb. Orange highlight on Box 5, the moment to add a print or pdb. A small note near Box 5: the module sees the real files, PATH and permissions. Bottom warning note in plain text: the kept folder holds the arguments you passed, so delete it when you finish. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Because you are on the target, the module sees the real files, the real PATH and the real permissions.
anchor: ## 6. Reproducing a module run by hand
alt: A module wrapper is kept on the target, unpacked with explode, and run with execute so its failure can be inspected on the host.
cap: Keeping the module wrapper on the target lets you unpack it and run it by hand, where you can see what the module actually saw.

name: a10-agent-forwarding
title: Why become breaks SSH agent forwarding for git
spec: A left-to-right chain with two lanes drawn as two rows. Top row, a path that works: a laptop box titled Your login session with a key icon labelled ssh-add -L, with the agent socket SSH_AUTH_SOCK inside it; an arrow labelled ForwardAgent=yes to a target box titled Target, running the git task with become: false; a tick and the note the clone works. Bottom row, the failing path: the same laptop box and the same forwarded agent arrow to a target box where the git task has become: true; an intermediate box titled sudo starts a clean environment with the note SSH_AUTH_SOCK is dropped unless env_keep keeps it; then a box with the note git has no agent to ask, leading to a result box labelled Permission denied (publickey). Orange highlight on the sudo box, the step that drops the variable. A small label at the bottom of the lower row: the key was fine, the environment was not. Monospace labels: SSH_AUTH_SOCK, ForwardAgent=yes, become: true, become: false, env_keep. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Check 3 is about privilege, and it is the one that catches most people, so make sure the git task does not set become: true.
alt: Agent forwarding works for a git task without become, but sudo drops the SSH_AUTH_SOCK variable when the task runs with become, so the clone fails.
cap: The forwarded SSH agent works only without become, because sudo starts a clean environment that drops the SSH_AUTH_SOCK variable.

name: a10-debugger-paths
title: Two ways to change a failed task in the debugger
spec: A top-to-bottom flow. Start box at the top: A task fails, and the (debug) prompt opens, with the note the task stays in memory. Below it, a split into two branches side by side. Left branch titled Change the argument: monospace command task.args['name'] = 'fixed', then an arrow to a box labelled r (redo), with the note re-runs the task with the change. Right branch titled Change the variable: monospace command task_vars['x'] = 1, then an arrow to a box labelled u (update_task), with the note re-templates task.args from the original expression, then an arrow down to a box labelled r (redo). Both branches meet at a bottom box labelled Task runs again. Side notes: p task.args, p task_vars and p result._result are shown as print commands above the split. Orange highlight on the update_task step, the one the right branch needs before redo takes effect. Below the diagram, a small table-like list of exit commands: c (continue) keeps the task failed; q (quit) aborts. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Use the debugger to experiment on one failing host, then write the fix into the playbook.
alt: In the task debugger you either edit the rendered arguments and redo, or edit a variable, run update_task and then redo.
cap: In the task debugger you can edit the rendered arguments and redo, or edit a variable, update the task, and then redo.

name: a10-group-failures
title: Grouping 200 failures into a short list of causes
spec: A left-to-right pipeline of five stations, each a box with a green number circle (1 to 5) above it, joined by orthogonal arrows. At the far left, a stack of log lines titled ansible-playbook output, drawn as many thin rows with FAILED and UNREACHABLE labels among them. Station 1: box labelled grep -E fatal:|FAILED with the note keeps only the failure lines. Station 2: box labelled sed s/.*=> // with the note strips the front of each line, leaving the message. Station 3: box labelled sort with the note puts identical messages next to each other. Station 4: box labelled uniq -c with the note counts each message. Station 5: box labelled sort -rn with the note lists the most common message first. At the far right, a ranked list of count and message rows, with the top row highlighted in orange. Monospace labels for each command. Below the pipeline, a note: examine one representative from each group, then sort the failing hosts by group, rack or OS. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Group the errors first, then examine a few representatives from each group.
anchor: ## 9. Debugging at scale and in CI
alt: A grep, sed, sort, uniq and sort pipeline turns a long list of failure lines into a ranked count of distinct error messages.
cap: A short shell pipeline groups many failure lines by message and ranks the most common message first.

name: a11-file-search
title: Where copy looks for a relative file inside a role
spec: A vertical stack of six numbered rows, each row a box with a green number circle on the left (1 to 6), arranged top to bottom with small downward arrows between them. Each box holds one monospace path: 1 ./roles/<role_name>/files/, 2 ./roles/<role_name>/, 3 ./roles/<role_name>/tasks/files/, 4 ./roles/<role_name>/tasks/, 5 ./files/ with the note adjacent to the top-level playbook, 6 ./ with the note the top-level playbook directory. On the far left, a task card in monospace: copy: src=pg_hba.conf. An arrow from the task card to row 1, labelled look here first. On the right side of the stack, a branch labelled file found, stop, with the note the first match wins, drawn from row 1 as an orange arrow. A second labelled note reads file not found, move on, drawn from rows 1 to 5 as a short arrow to the next row. The orange highlight is on row 1, the role's own files/ folder, which wins over the playbook's folder. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: The order matters when two folders hold a file with the same name, and the role's own files/ folder wins.
alt: A copy task searches six paths in order inside and around the role and stops at the first file it finds.
cap: A relative file name in a role is searched in six locations, and the first match wins.

name: a11-role-run-order
title: Where roles, import_role and include_role run in a play
spec: A horizontal sequence of four section boxes across the top, left to right, with orthogonal arrows: pre_tasks, then a middle box titled roles and tasks, then post_tasks. The middle box is split into two sub-rows: the top sub-row is the roles: list, labelled classic, runs before tasks; below it a task flow with a small card labelled ansible.builtin.import_role marked static, fixed at parse time, and a card labelled ansible.builtin.include_role marked dynamic, decided at runtime, with a loop icon and the note supports loop and tasks_from. Above the sequence, a thin bar with three labelled markers: Parse time for import_role, Runtime for include_role. Below the sequence, green note-chips listing the common handler behaviour: Handlers flush between sections. Orange highlight on include_role, the one that can run a role after a reboot or a drain step. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Use roles: for simple cases, and the other two for mid-task roles.
alt: A play runs pre_tasks, then roles and tasks in order, then post_tasks, and import_role is fixed at parse time while include_role decides at runtime.
cap: A play runs its pre_tasks first, then roles and tasks, then post_tasks, and only include_role can sit in the middle of the task flow and decide at runtime.

name: a11-gpu-order
title: Role order on a bare-metal GPU node
spec: A vertical or left-to-right stack of six stage boxes, each with a green number circle (1 to 6) and an arrow to the next stage. Stage 1 box, titled base OS and kernel: role common_base for repos, time sync with chrony, SSH and sudo hardening, users and storage mounts; and role kernel_tuning for the pinned kernel, sysctls, hugepages, kernel modules and the nouveau blacklist. Stage 2 box, titled drivers: gpu_facts and gpu_driver for the NVIDIA driver, nvidia-persistenced, Fabric Manager on NVSwitch nodes, MIG configuration and nvidia-smi validation. Stage 3 box, titled container runtime: container_runtime and nvidia_container_toolkit for containerd or Docker, and the nvidia-ctk CDI or runtime hook. Stage 4 box, titled monitoring: monitoring_agents for node_exporter and dcgm-exporter. Stage 5 box, titled scheduler or Kubernetes agents: slurm_client or kubelet, with the note joins the cluster. Stage 6 at the end: a gate box labelled only after every GPU and runtime validation has passed. Orange highlight on Stage 5 and its gate, the step that joins the node to the cluster. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Document this order in the playbook, not in hidden role dependencies.
anchor: ## 7. Role patterns specific to GPU infrastructure
alt: A GPU node gets its base OS and kernel first, then drivers, the container runtime, monitoring, and finally the scheduler agent after validation.
cap: On a GPU node the base OS and kernel come first, the scheduler agent joins last, and only after every GPU and runtime check has passed.

name: a11-collection-path
title: From collection skeleton to published package
spec: A left-to-right flow of five boxes joined by orthogonal arrows, each with a green number circle (1 to 5). Box 1: init, with the monospace command ansible-galaxy collection init acme.gpu and the note creates the skeleton. Box 2: build, with the monospace command ansible-galaxy collection build and the note creates acme-gpu-1.4.0.tar.gz. Box 3: install locally, with the monospace command ansible-galaxy collection install ./acme-gpu-1.4.0.tar.gz -p collections/ and the note catches a missing file before anyone else sees it. Box 4: test, shown as three stacked small boxes labelled sanity, units and integration, with the notes style, docs and imports; small units of Python functions; runs against a real target. Box 5: publish, with the monospace command ansible-galaxy collection publish acme-gpu-1.4.0.tar.gz --server automation_hub. Below Box 3 a small orange note: this step is the one people skip. Below the whole flow, a single note in monospace: galaxy.yml holds namespace, name, version and dependencies. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Installing the tarball locally before publishing is the step people skip, and it is the one that catches a missing file.
alt: A collection is initialised, built into a tarball, installed locally, tested with three ansible-test suites, and then published.
cap: A collection goes from skeleton to published tarball in five steps, and the local install step catches a missing file before anyone else sees it.

name: a12-vault-indirection
title: Plaintext pointers in one file, encrypted values in another
spec: Two file cards side by side with a bold connector between them. Left card, a plaintext file with a green check icon, titled group_vars/all/vars.yml, marked reviewed in PRs. Inside it three monospace rows: db_password: "{{ vault_db_password }}", registry_token: "{{ vault_registry_token }}", slurm_munge_key_b64: "{{ vault_munge_key_b64 }}". Right card, a locked box icon, titled group_vars/all/vault.yml, marked encrypted. Inside it three monospace rows, each with the value shown as a sealed block: vault_db_password, vault_registry_token, vault_munge_key_b64, with the values drawn as hidden ciphertext bars. Between the two cards, orthogonal arrows from each left row to the matching right row, each arrow labelled points to. Above the connector, a small note in plain text: a reviewer reads the names in a pull request and never sees the values. Below both cards, two small monospace notes: grep -r db_password shows where the secret is used, and ansible-vault view shows the vault names. Orange highlight on the arrow from db_password to vault_db_password. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: The label is public, and the drawer is not.
alt: A plaintext vars file points each variable at a vault_ name in an encrypted vault file, so reviewers can read the names without seeing the values.
cap: The plaintext vars file points each variable at a vault_ name, while the values stay encrypted in a separate vault file.

name: a12-vault-ids
title: Vault IDs keep dev and prod passwords apart
spec: Two vertical lanes side by side, each with a lane title: dev on the left and prod on the right. Left lane: a key card labelled dev@~/.vault_pass_dev in monospace, an arrow down to a box titled group_vars/dev/vault.yml with the header note $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.2;AES256;dev, and a tick with the label opens. Right lane: a key card labelled prod@prompt in monospace, an arrow down to a box titled group_vars/prod/vault.yml with the header note $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.2;AES256;prod, and a tick with the label opens. A dashed orange X between the lanes, labelled dev password cannot open prod, drawn as the single important item. Above both lanes, a single box with the monospace line vault_identity_list = dev@~/.vault_pass_dev, prod@~/.vault_pass_prod, with a note the playbook run loads both keys without flags. At the bottom of the prod lane, a small note: the prod password stays with fewer people, or only with the CI or AAP credential store. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Separate passwords per environment mean a developer with dev access cannot decrypt prod.
alt: Each environment's vault file names its own vault ID in its header, so the dev password cannot open the prod file.
cap: Each vault file records its own label, so a developer holding only the dev password cannot open the prod file.

name: a12-leak-paths
title: Where a secret can leak and the control that closes each path
spec: A two-column map. Left column titled Leak path, with six stacked boxes, each with a small warning icon: --diff and -v output; a register followed by a later debug of that result; command or shell arguments, visible in ps and shell history; an Environment= line in a world-readable unit file; fact caching that keeps a secret saved as a fact; module errors that echo arguments. Right column titled Control, with six matching boxes connected to each leak by orthogonal arrows: diff: false and no_log: true; no_log: true on the sensitive task; pass the value through a file with mode 0600, through stdin, or through environment:; EnvironmentFile= with mode 0600 or 0640 and the right owner; cacheable: false and a protected cache directory; prefer no_log over trusting the module. Monospace labels for each setting name. Orange highlight on the command or shell arrow, the path that shows the secret in ps. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Treat no_log: true and diff: false as the default for any task that handles a secret.
alt: Each leak path for a secret, such as diff output, registered results, command arguments or unit files, has a matching control.
cap: Each place a secret can leak, from diff output to unit files, has a specific setting that closes it.

name: a12-two-phase-rotation
title: Two-phase overlap rotation with no downtime
spec: A horizontal timeline with three phase columns left to right, each with a green number circle and a bold title. Phase 1 titled Expand: a provider box with two key tokens, v1 and v2, both drawn valid at the same time; the note create a second valid credential, such as user_v2 or a secondary API key or cert. Phase 2 titled Roll consumers: a row of consumer boxes labelled app nodes, drawn as server icons, each switching to v2, with a monospace note ansible rolling update with serial, and a verify health tick. Phase 3 titled Contract: the provider box with v1 struck through and v2 kept, with the note once every consumer is verified on v2 and connection logs show zero v1 use, revoke or drop v1 on the provider. Orange highlight on Phase 3, the step that removes the old credential. Above the timeline, a thin bar labelled both valid, no downtime spanning Phase 1 and Phase 2. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: Add the new credential, deploy the consumers, then remove the old one.
alt: Two-phase rotation first adds a second valid credential, then rolls every consumer to it, and only then revokes the old one.
cap: Two-phase rotation adds a second valid credential, moves every consumer over, and only then revokes the old one.

name: a13-molecule-sequence
title: The Molecule test sequence and where a failure points
spec: A horizontal row of step boxes from left to right, joined by arrows in time order and numbered with number circles 1 to 6. Each box has a simple outline icon above its title. Box 1 create, icon disk cylinder. Box 2 converge, icon gear. Box 3 idempotence, icon clock, drawn with an orange outline because it finds the majority of subtle bugs. Box 4 verify, icon shield. Box 5 destroy, icon window. Two optional steps are drawn as dashed boxes: prepare, placed between create and converge, and side_effect, placed between idempotence and verify. Under each box a short note line in secondary text. Under create: failure is about the image or Docker itself, the role has not run yet. Under converge: failure is about the role's first run. Under idempotence: the role ran once, then changed something on the second run. Under verify: the role ran, but the result is not what the check expected. Above the row, a label line: molecule test runs the whole sequence in one go. No takeaway bar.
alt: Molecule runs create, converge, idempotence and verify in order, and a failure at each step points to a different cause.
cap: Each Molecule stage has its own failure meaning, so the failing step name tells you which part of the role to inspect.

name: a13-ci-job-graph
title: The Ansible CI workflow: lint gates the Molecule matrix
spec: One large container labelled ansible-ci workflow. Inside it three job boxes in a row, with equal spacing. Left box lint with a shield icon, runs-on ubuntu-latest, step line: yamllint . && ansible-lint. Middle box molecule with a gear icon, a matrix line showing role: kernel_tuning, chrony_client, dcgm_exporter and distro: ubuntu2204, rockylinux9, step line: molecule test. Right box gpu-hw with a chip icon, runs-on self-hosted, gpu, step line: molecule test -s gpu_hw. Draw ONE solid arrow from lint to molecule, labelled needs: lint. No arrow goes to gpu-hw. Under the gpu-hw box a note in secondary text: runs on schedule (nightly cron 0 4 * * *) or when a pull request has the test-gpu label. Under the molecule box a note: a broken file never starts a container. No takeaway bar.
alt: In the CI workflow the lint job runs first, the Molecule matrix waits for it, and the GPU job runs on a schedule or label.
cap: The Molecule jobs wait for lint, so a broken file never starts a container, and the GPU tier runs on its own schedule.

name: a14-linear-vs-free
title: linear waits at each task for the slowest host, free lets healthy hosts run on
spec: Two side-by-side panels. Left panel titled strategy: linear with a chain icon. Inside it two horizontal lanes, one labelled healthy host and one labelled slow host. The healthy lane finishes its first task block early and then sits idle. The slow lane's first task block is longer. A vertical barrier line sits at the end of the first task block in both lanes, labelled wait for slowest host. Only after the barrier does the second task block start in both lanes. Under the panel, a label: each task runs on all hosts in the batch before the next task starts. Right panel titled strategy: free with a runner icon. Two lanes with the same blocks, but there is no barrier: the healthy lane runs straight on into its second task block and finishes early, and the slow lane finishes later. Under the panel, a label: each host runs through the play at its own pace. Orange note on the linear panel: every task waits for the slowest host. Number circles 1 and 2 on the task blocks of the linear panel to show time order. No takeaway bar.
alt: Under linear every task waits for the slowest host, while under free healthy hosts run on at their own pace.
cap: With linear every task waits for the slowest host, while free lets healthy hosts finish early.

name: a14-async-background-job
title: async with poll 0: the job runs in the background while the controller checks later
spec: A sequence diagram with three vertical swimlanes side by side, each with a header: Controller (Ansible), Rack host, Background job. Number circles 1 to 5 mark messages in top-to-bottom time order. Message 1, horizontal arrow from Controller to Rack host, labelled command with async: 3600 and poll: 0. Message 2, a short arrow from Rack host to Background job labelled starts in the background. Message 3, arrow from Rack host back to Controller labelled returns a job ID and moves on at once. A shaded vertical span between messages 3 and 4 in the Controller lane is labelled no SSH session needs to stay open, drawn in orange as the key point. Message 4, arrow from Controller to Rack host labelled async_status with until: fw_result.finished, delay: 30 and retries: 120. Message 5, arrow from Rack host back to Controller labelled finished. Use the monospace font for the code-like labels. Under the Background job lane a small label: allowed runtime 3600 seconds. No takeaway bar.
alt: A background job runs on the host while the controller returns at once, then polls with async_status until it finishes.
cap: With async and poll set to 0 the controller does not hold an SSH session open, and it checks the job later with async_status.

name: a14-ring-promotion
title: Rings: a change is promoted from the canary branch to stable
spec: Three ring boxes in a left-to-right row with equal spacing and an arrow between each neighbour. Each box has a simple outline icon above its title, a stack of nodes for the ring and a git branch icon for the branch. Box 1 titled Ring 0 with a branch label canary. Box 2 titled ring 1 with branch label stable-1. Box 3 titled ring 2 with branch label stable. Number circles 1, 2 and 3 on the boxes for the order of promotion. Arrow from box 1 to box 2 labelled fast-forward after validation passes. Arrow from box 2 to box 3 with the same label. Ring 0 box drawn with an orange outline because the change lands there first. Above Ring 0, a small label: a change lands on canary. Below the three boxes, a short text line: promote by fast-forwarding the branches, or by moving signed tags. Monospace text for the branch names. No takeaway bar.
alt: A change lands on the canary branch for ring 0, then moves to stable-1 and stable after each ring validates it.
cap: Rings promote a change one stage at a time, so each ring validates it before the next ring receives it.

name: a15-module-idempotency-loop
title: A module reads, compares, changes only if needed, and reports changed
spec: A horizontal row of four step boxes left to right, joined by arrows in time order, with number circles 1 to 4. Each box has a simple outline icon above its title. Box 1, title Read the current state, icon gauge. Box 2, title compute the difference, icon balance scale or two overlapping squares. Box 3, title change only if needed, icon gear, drawn with the orange outline because it is the step that must not run when nothing differs. Box 4, title report changed accurately, icon clock or checkmark in a window. Under box 3 a short note line: runs only when the state differs. Below the row, a green panel titled Thermostat with a thermostat icon and three short lines of secondary text: reads the room temperature; compares it with the setting; turns the heater on only when the room is too cold. Draw a thin dotted line from each thermostat line up to the matching step box, so the analogy maps onto the four steps. No takeaway bar.
alt: A module reads the current state, computes the difference, changes only if needed, and reports changed accurately.
cap: An idempotent module reads the current state first and changes the system only when the state differs from the request.

name: a15-module-test-ladder
title: Five steps to test a module, from simplest to most complete
spec: A staircase of five steps rising from bottom left to top right, with equal step width. Each step is a box with a number circle (1 to 5) at its left, a simple outline icon and a title, plus one line of secondary text for what that step catches. Step 1, title Run the module directly, icon terminal window, text: catches crashes in the logic before Ansible is involved. Step 2, title Run it ad hoc, icon gear, text: checks that Ansible passes the arguments and reads the result. Step 3, title Write unit tests with pytest, icon checklist, text: runs without a GPU, using a mock. Step 4, title Run ansible-test sanity, icon shield, text: checks documentation and style. Step 5, title Run the module twice, icon two looping arrows, drawn with the orange outline, text: the second run reports changed as false. Arrows: a single thin arrow runs up the staircase from step 1 to step 5, labelled simplest to most complete. Monospace text for the commands in the titles where they appear. No takeaway bar.
alt: Five testing steps climb from running the module directly to running it twice and confirming changed is false.
cap: Each of the five test steps catches a different kind of mistake, so you should not skip ahead.

name: a15-eda-remediation-flow
title: An EDA rule hands remediation to a job template
spec: A left-to-right flow of four boxes joined by three solid arrows, numbered 1 to 4 in time order. Box 1, icon bell, title Alertmanager source on port 5000, sub-label alert GPUXid79 firing. Box 2, icon rulebook or scroll, title rule Cordon on Xid 79, sub-label condition matches. Box 3, icon window, title run_job_template drain-and-diagnose-node, monospace sub-label target_node from the alert. Box 4, icon server, title managed node. Arrow 1 to 2 labelled condition matches.
