Under box 3, a dashed callout box containing three short lines: credentials, Execution Environment, approval rules, with a note that the rule itself does not do the work. Keep the callout outside the arrow path so no arrow crosses it. No takeaway bar.
alt: An EDA rule matches a firing GPUXid79 alert and launches the drain-and-diagnose-node job template on the node.
cap: An EDA rule hands the remediation to a job template, which holds the credentials and approval rules rather than the rule itself.

name: a16-network-connection
title: Network modules run on the controller and reach the device through a connection
spec: Two large boxes side by side with a wide gap between them. The left box, titled Controller, has a laptop or window icon and a secondary line: the playbook runs here. Inside it a sub-box with a gear icon and the text: turns the desired state into commands or RPCs. The right box, titled Network device, has a switch icon and a secondary line: no Python needed on the device. Numbered circles 1 and 2 mark the order: 1 on the controller box, 2 on the arrow. One solid arrow runs from the controller box to the device box across the gap, labelled with three lines of monospace text: ansible.netcommon.network_cli, ansible.netcommon.netconf, ansible.netcommon.httpapi, and with the small caption: connection options. Draw the arrow once only. Above the arrow, a small label: ansible_network_os names the platform. Under the two boxes, a green note panel with a translator icon and one line: a translator outside a locked office, which cannot go inside but speaks the receptionist's language. Orange outline on the arrow because the connection is the key link. No takeaway bar.
alt: Network modules run on the controller, turn the desired state into commands, and reach the device through a network connection plugin.
cap: Network modules run on the control node and reach the device through a connection plugin, because the device usually cannot run Python.

name: a16-cluster-boundary
title: The cluster boundary decides which tool owns each layer
spec: A vertical stack of two large panels separated by one horizontal dashed line in orange, labelled cluster boundary, drawn across the full width. Upper panel, titled Kubernetes workloads, with a cluster or container icon, and a secondary line: GitOps keeps this layer reconciled. Inside the upper panel a small box with a sync-arrows icon labelled Argo CD or Flux. Lower panel, titled Ansible owns the layer beneath the cluster, with a gear icon. Inside the lower panel five equal rows, each with a small icon and a label: node preparation; cluster bootstrap with Kubespray or kubeadm; initial platform installs such as the CNI, the GPU Operator and Argo CD itself; certificate and kubeconfig distribution; day-2 node operations such as cordon, drain and upgrade. Right of the lower panel, a short label box: Ansible owns the layer beneath the cluster. Left of the upper panel, a short label box: GitOps owns what runs inside it. Green takeaway bar at the bottom with the text: Ansible owns the layer beneath the cluster, and GitOps owns what runs inside it.
alt: Above the cluster boundary GitOps reconciles workloads, while Ansible handles the node, bootstrap, platform installs and day-2 operations below it.
cap: Ansible handles the layer beneath the cluster and GitOps handles what runs inside it, and the cluster boundary decides which tool to use.

name: a17-reload-or-reboot
title: Reload the GPU modules when you can, and fall back to a reboot when a holder blocks the unload
spec: A top-down flow drawn left to right with numbered steps, joined by solid arrows. Start box at the left titled Driver upgrade, icon gear, with the note: decide reload or reboot before the upgrade starts. Step 1 box: Stop the dependent services, icon window, a sub-line listing DCGM, persistenced, exporters and containers. Step 2 box: Unload the modules, icon chip, monospace text: nvidia_uvm, nvidia_drm, nvidia_modeset, nvidia, with the note in order from the top of the stack down. A decision diamond after step 2 labelled Unload succeeds? Yes arrow goes right to Step 3 box: Load the new modules with modprobe, icon shield, then to an end box titled Node stays up. No arrow goes down from the diamond to a box titled Find the holders, icon magnifier, with monospace text: lsof /dev/nvidia* or fuser -v /dev/nvidia*. From Find the holders, an arrow goes right to a decision diamond labelled Still fails? Yes arrow goes right to a box titled Reboot, icon power button, drawn with the orange outline, with the note: slower, but leaves no half-unloaded state. The No arrow from Still fails? goes back up to Step 3 box. Number circles 1, 2, 3 on steps 1 to 3. Monospace text for the module names and commands. No takeaway bar.
anchor: ## 4. Reboots, long tasks and idempotent upgrades
alt: Modules are unloaded top down and reloaded, and when a process holds a device open the node falls back to a reboot.
cap: A module reload avoids a reboot when nothing holds the device, and a reboot is the safe fallback when the unload still fails.

name: a17-drain-patch-resume
title: Drain, patch, validate and resume one node at a time
spec: A left-to-right workflow with numbered steps in time order, joined by solid arrows. A band above the flow, labelled serial, shows the batch sizes in three small boxes: 1 node first as the canary, then 5%, then 10%. Step 1 box, icon gate or stop sign: Drain from Slurm, with monospace text scontrol update NodeName=... State=DRAIN. Step 2 box, icon clock: Wait for jobs to finish, with monospace text squeue -h -w ... repeated until empty. Step 3 box, icon gear: Apply updates, with two stacked sub-boxes labelled import_role nvidia_driver and gpu_validate quick. A decision diamond after step 3 labelled Validation passes? Yes arrow goes right to step 4 box, icon checkmark: Return to service, with monospace text scontrol update NodeName=... State=RESUME. No arrow goes down from the diamond to a red-outlined box, drawn in the orange outline, titled rescue: leave node DRAINED, with the sub-line: then fail, requires investigation. Under the rescue box, a small note: a drained node keeps its running jobs but takes no new ones. Under the whole flow, a note: max_fail_percentage 3 stops the rollout past 3 percent failures. No takeaway bar.
alt: Each node is drained, waits for its jobs, is patched and validated, then returns to service, and stays drained if validation fails.
cap: A node returns to Slurm only after its jobs finish and validation passes, and a failed node stays drained for investigation.

name: a18-plan-symbols
title: Reading the symbols in a Terraform plan
spec: A legend laid out as six equal rows stacked top to bottom, each row a horizontal strip with a large monospace symbol chip on the left, a bold title in the middle and one line of secondary text on the right. Row 1: chip + , title create, text: the resource will be created. Row 2: chip ~, title update in place, text: the change is made without destroying the object. Row 3: chip -, title destroy, text: the object is deleted. Row 4: chip -/+, title destroy and then create, text: forces replacement. Row 5: chip +/-, title create and then destroy, text: appears with create_before_destroy. Row 6: chip <=, title read, text: a data source is read. Draw the row 4 strip with the orange outline, because replacement of a stateful object is the change to question. Below the six rows, a green panel with the summary line in monospace: Plan: X to add, Y to change, Z to destroy. Under the panel, a short line: look for unexpected destroys and replacements first. No arrows. No takeaway bar.
alt: A Terraform plan marks create with plus, update in place with tilde, destroy with minus, and replacement with minus-plus or plus-minus.
cap: The plan symbols tell you whether Terraform creates, updates, destroys or replaces each object, and replacements deserve the closest reading.

name: a18-moved-block
title: A moved block turns a rename into a move instead of a destroy and create
spec: Two horizontal paths stacked in two bands, with a label on the left of each band. Top band labelled without a moved block. From the left, a state box with a disk cylinder icon holding the entry google_compute_network.fabric, then a box labelled config address module.network.google_compute_network.this. Two arrows leave the state box and the config box toward a destroy box and a create box on the right. The arrow from state to the destroy box is labelled no matching config. The arrow from config to the create box is labelled no state entry. The destroy box is drawn with the orange outline and carries the note: an outage for a network or a database. Bottom band labelled with a moved block. The same state box and the same config box, joined by one arrow labelled moved from ... to ... in monospace, ending at a result box with a checkmark icon labelled has moved, with the note nothing is destroyed. Show the moved block code under the bottom band in monospace: moved { from = google_compute_network.fabric, to = module.network.google_compute_network.this }. No takeaway bar.
alt: Without a moved block a rename destroys and recreates the network, while a moved block keeps the same object under its new name.
cap: A moved block tells Terraform that a renamed resource is the same object, so the plan shows a move rather than a destroy and create.

name: a18-terraform-ansible-handoff
title: Terraform renders the inventory file that Ansible reads
spec: A left-to-right flow in two labelled zones. A large container on the left titled Terraform decides which machines exist and what they are called, holding three boxes stacked and connected to a fourth box on the right. Box A: random_pet.cluster, icon dice, sub-label length = 2. Box B: var.nodes, icon list, sub-label gpu01 gpus=8, gpu02 gpus=8, gpu03 gpus=4. Box C: local_file.inventory, icon document, sub-label templatefile() renders inventory.tftpl. Arrow from box A to box C labelled cluster name, arrow from box B to box C labelled nodes. Box D on the far right: inventory.ini, icon file with a handoff arrow, drawn with the orange outline and the note the rendered file is the handoff. An arrow from box C to box D labelled rendered. A separate zone on the far right, beside box D, titled Ansible decides what runs on them, with a gear icon, connected to box D by a dotted arrow. Number circles 1 to 3 on boxes A, B and C to show the order of evaluation. Monospace text for the resource and file names. No takeaway bar.
alt: Terraform renders a local file from a random cluster name and a node list, and the inventory file becomes the handoff to Ansible.
cap: Terraform renders the inventory file from its own state and inputs, and Ansible reads that file to decide what runs on each machine.

name: a19-move-resource-states
title: Move a resource between states without destroying it
spec: Two tall panels side by side, left panel titled State A (the old owner), right panel titled State B (the new owner). A bucket-shaped storage icon sits in each panel's centre area, labelled aws_s3_bucket.checkpoints, drawn once in State A and once in State B. Four numbered circles (1 to 4) run top to bottom down the middle. Step 1, inside State B: a box reading 'Add the resource configuration and an import block', with the monospace text import { to = aws_s3_bucket.checkpoints }. Step 2, an arrow from step 1 into a box reading 'Apply B, so it tracks the resource', with the bucket arrow pointing from State B into the bucket. Step 3, inside State A: a box reading 'Add a removed block with destroy = false and apply A', with the monospace text removed { lifecycle { destroy = false } }, and an arrow reading 'Tells A to let go without touching the bucket'. Step 4, inside State A: a box reading 'Delete the code from A'. Orange outline on the step 3 box, as the single most important step. Under the panels, a green note: 'Check that both plans are clean at each step, because a dirty plan at any step means two states are now fighting over one object.' Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Think of it as adding the new owner before removing the old one.' No arrowheads between the two panels other than the bucket arrows.
anchor: ### Split or merge states, rename resources
alt: Four steps move an S3 bucket from state A to state B: import into B, apply B, removed with destroy false in A, then delete the code from A.
cap: Moving a resource between states takes four steps, and the bucket is never destroyed.

name: a19-drift-decision
title: Decide what to do with each drift item
spec: Top: a box with a clock or alert icon titled 'Drift found', text 'terraform plan shows a difference between the config and the real world'. An arrow down to a decision box titled 'Decide case by case', with a gear or branch icon, outlined in orange as the single most important item. Three arrows leave the decision box to the right, one per card, arranged as three columns. Card 1, title 'Revert the drift', icon: a rewind arrow, text 'Apply the intended config, when the hotfix was temporary'. Card 2, title 'Adopt the drift', icon: a pencil or document icon, text 'Edit the config to match, so the plan comes back clean, when the hotfix is the new truth'. Card 3, title 'Tolerate the drift', icon: a shield icon, text 'Use lifecycle { ignore_changes = [...] } for fields managed elsewhere', with the example 'such as an autoscaler-managed desired_size or labels added by controllers'. Under the cards, a green note: 'Decide, for each drift item, whether to revert, adopt or tolerate it before the next apply.' No number circles, since the three options are not in time order.
alt: Drift can be reverted by applying the config, adopted by editing the config, or tolerated with ignore_changes.
cap: For each drift item you either revert it, adopt it into the config, or tolerate it with ignore_changes.

name: a20-validation-flow
title: A validation rule stops a bad GPU count before planning
spec: A left-to-right flow of numbered steps (number circles 1 to 5, green). Step 1: a box with a person or form icon titled 'Caller sets gpu_count', text 'Caller sets gpu_count to 3'. Arrow to step 2: a box with a shield or check icon titled 'Condition checks the list', text 'Is 3 in [0, 1, 2, 4, 8]?' with the answer 'No' on the arrow. Step 3, orange outline (the most important step): a box with an alert icon titled 'Validation fails', showing the monospace error line 'gpu_count must be 0, 1, 2, 4 or 8.' Arrow from step 3 back down to step 4: a box with a pencil icon titled 'Caller changes the value', text 'Set gpu_count to 4 or 8'. Arrow to step 5: a box with a clock or gear icon titled 'The plan goes on', text 'Plan continues'. Beside the list box, a short green note: 'The list stands in for the node shapes your platform team supports.' Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Validation runs during planning, so the caller fixes the value before anything is created.' No arrow crosses another arrow.
alt: A gpu_count of 3 fails the validation list check during planning, so the caller changes it to 4 or 8.
cap: A validation block rejects an unsupported GPU count during planning, before any infrastructure is created.

name: a20-promote-pin
title: Promote a module pin one environment at a time
spec: Top row of two numbered steps (number circles 1 and 2). Step 1 box with a document icon titled 'Read the changelog', text 'Then run terraform init -upgrade in a branch', with the monospace text terraform init -upgrade. Step 2 box with a magnifier icon titled 'Plan the lower environments first', text 'Confirm there are no unexpected replacements', with the monospace text must be replaced. Below, a horizontal row of three environment boxes connected left to right by arrows: 'dev', then 'staging', then 'prod'. Each environment box has a small pin icon and the text 'Promote the version pin'. Between each pair of environment boxes, a small diamond decision labelled 'Unexpected replacement?'. The No path continues to the next environment. The Yes path, drawn in orange as the single most important path, leads down to a stop box with a hand or stop icon titled 'Stop', with the note 'Stopping is a success, not a failure.' Under the environment row, a box numbered 3 titled 'Promote the version pin through dev, staging and prod'. Box numbered 4 at the far right, titled 'For breaking changes', text 'Ship a migration guide, moved blocks and deprecation periods'. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'The plan has just saved you from rebuilding a stateful resource.' No other arrows.
alt: Upgrade a module by reading the changelog, planning lower environments, promoting the pin in order, and stopping at any unexpected replacement.
cap: A module upgrade moves from dev to staging to prod, and the rollout stops the moment a plan shows an unexpected replacement.

name: a20-provider-alias
title: Pass a regional provider into each module call
spec: Top panel titled 'Root module' containing two provider blocks side by side as cards with a cloud icon each. Left card: monospace 'provider google', 'alias = us', 'region = us-central1'. Right card: monospace 'provider google', 'alias = eu', 'region = europe-west4'. Below the panel, two module call boxes side by side. Left: 'module pool_us' with monospace 'providers = { google = google.us }'. Right: 'module pool_eu' with monospace 'providers = { google = google.eu }'. Arrows drawn from the 'alias = us' card down to the pool_us box, and from the 'alias = eu' card down to the pool_eu box, so the two arrows do not cross. Both module boxes point into one shared box at the bottom titled 'gke-gpu-pool', with the note 'Same module code builds both pools'. Orange outline on the note 'You cannot choose a provider per instance inside for_each, because provider mappings are static.' placed at the bottom right. Under it, two options in green cards: 'Repeat the module call for each region' and 'Use a separate stack per region'. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Decide which of the two you want before the platform grows.' No number circles, since these are not in time order.
alt: Two google providers, one per region, are passed into two calls of the same gke-gpu-pool module.
cap: Each module call receives one regional provider, so the same module code can build pools in two regions.

name: a21-count-vs-foreach
title: Removing one item from the middle: count versus for_each
spec: Two side-by-side panels with a green heading each. Left panel titled 'count (index is identity)'. Top row shows a list of three boxes indexed [0], [1], [2] with the names a100-train, h100-train, a100-infer. The middle box h100-train is struck through and removed with a dashed outline. Below, a row of arrows showing a100-infer sliding from index [2] down to index [1]. Outcome boxes: one orange-outlined box (the most important item) reading 'a100-infer is replaced' and a grey box reading 'the index [1] now names a different pool'. Right panel titled 'for_each (key is identity)'. Top row shows three boxes labelled with keys a100-train, h100-train, a100-infer (the keys shown as names in quotes, no indexes). The h100-train box is removed with a dashed outline. Nothing else moves. Outcome box in green reading 'Only h100-train is destroyed' and a second green box reading 'a100-infer is untouched'. Use a disk-stack or gear icon on each box. No number circles, since the boxes are not steps in time order. Under both panels, a green note: 'Use count only when you would never tell two instances apart.' Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'If each instance has a name you care about, use for_each with stable keys.' Arrows: only the slide arrow in the left panel, no crossing arrows.
alt: Removing a middle item shifts indexes under count and replaces a later pool, while for_each destroys only the removed key.
cap: Removing a middle item under count shifts later indexes and replaces a pool nobody touched, while for_each destroys only the removed key.

name: a21-lifecycle-order
title: Order of checks and replacement under lifecycle
spec: A left-to-right sequence of four numbered steps (green number circles 1 to 4). Step 1: a box with a clipboard icon titled 'precondition', showing the condition data.aws_ec2_instance_type.selected.default_vcpus >= 16 in monospace and the message 'Login nodes need at least 16 vCPUs.' A small note under step 1: 'The check runs before creation.' Arrow to step 2: a box with a plus or new-node icon titled 'Create the replacement first', with the label 'create_before_destroy = true'. Arrow to step 3: a box with a trash or minus icon titled 'Destroy the old one', text 'Creates its replacement before destroying the old one'. Arrow to step 4: a box with a magnifier icon titled 'postcondition', showing the condition self.public_ip == "" in monospace and the message 'Login nodes must not have public IPs.' Orange outline on step 4 as the single most important check. A small green note under step 4: 'A node that comes up with a public address fails the run.' Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Preconditions guard the input, postconditions guard the result.'
alt: A login node runs its precondition, creates a replacement before destroying the old node, then checks its postcondition.
cap: Under the lifecycle block, the precondition runs before creation, the replacement is created before the old node is destroyed, and the postcondition checks the result.

name: a21-if-else-index-trap
title: The if/else [0] index trap and the one(concat()) fix
spec: Top section: two resource boxes stacked vertically, each with a cloud or user icon. Upper box: monospace 'neo_cloudwatch_full_access', with the label 'count = var.give_neo_cloudwatch_full_access ? 1 : 0'. Lower box: monospace 'neo_cloudwatch_read_only', with the label 'count = var.give_neo_cloudwatch_full_access ? 0 : 1'. Note inside each box: for any input exactly one of the two lists is empty. Arrows from both boxes into one box titled 'Output reads [0] from each list', with the monospace text full_access[0].policy_arn in one branch and read_only[0].policy_arn in the other. An alert icon beside this box in orange (the single most important item) with the error text 'index 0 out of range for list of length 0'. Bottom section, titled 'Fix', one green box with the monospace text one(concat(full_access[*].policy_arn, read_only[*].policy_arn)) and the note 'The concat joins the two splat lists, and one() returns the single element or null'. No number circles, since these are not in time order. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Splat both lists and let one() pick, so no branch reads index zero from an empty list.'
alt: Two opposite count toggles leave one list empty, so reading index zero fails; one of concat with one fixes it.
cap: Two opposite count toggles leave one list empty, so the output should combine the splat lists with concat and one instead of reading index zero.

name: a22-strategy-ladder
title: Pick the first secret strategy your provider supports
spec: A descending staircase or ladder of seven numbered steps (green number circles 1 to 7), with step 1 at the top left and step 7 at the bottom right, each step a wide box with one outline icon. Step 1, key-off or identity badge icon, title 'Avoid secrets altogether', text 'Prefer identity-based access over passwords and keys'. Step 2, cloud with lock icon, title 'Let the target service generate and store the secret', text 'Terraform stores only the secret reference'. Step 3, empty box with lock icon, title 'Create the secret container, not the value', text 'A CI step, an operator or a rotation job sets the value out of band'. Step 4, clock or sparkle icon, title 'Ephemeral and write-only features', text 'Values exist only during the run'. Step 5, secret manager or cloud icon, title 'Read the value at apply time', text 'A data source reads it from a secret manager'. Step 6, shield icon, title 'Encrypt state', text 'Backend encryption, and client-side encryption in OpenTofu'. Step 7, orange outline (the last resort, drawn as the single most important warning), terminal or environment variable icon, title 'Environment variables', text 'Pass TF_VAR_db_password from the CI secret store and accept that it ends up in state'. Above the staircase, a green note: 'Work down the list until one fits your case.' Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'The first strategy that your provider and version support is usually the right one.'
alt: Seven secret strategies ordered from best to worst, ending with environment variables as the last resort.
cap: Seven secret strategies run from best to worst, and the first one your provider and version supports is usually the right choice.

name: a22-federated-auth
title: Short-lived federated credentials instead of stored keys
spec: Left to right flow with four numbered steps (number circles 1 to 4, green). Step 1: a box with a CI pipeline or runner icon titled 'CI job', text 'Runs terraform plan'. Arrow to step 2: a box with an id-card or badge icon titled 'Signed token from its own identity provider', text 'The CI system proves who it is'. Arrow to step 3: a box with a shield or policy icon titled 'The cloud checks the trust', text 'Trust policy conditions on repo, branch and environment'. Arrow to step 4: a box with a clock icon titled 'Temporary credential for one role', text 'Short-lived, valid only for one role, expires before anyone can misuse it'. The arrow into step 3 is orange, as the single most important check. Above the flow, a note: 'No key is stored in the repo or in CI variables.' Below the flow, two small boxes side by side: 'AWS: assume_role in provider' and 'GCP: impersonate_service_account' showing where the role is named. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'The caller stays the same, and the permission comes from the role.' Monospace label in step 3: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.
alt: A CI job presents a signed identity token, the cloud checks the trust conditions, and returns a short-lived role credential.
cap: A CI job trades its own signed identity token for a short-lived credential for one role, so no static key is stored.

name: a22-layered-k8s
title: Create the cluster in one stack, configure Kubernetes in the next
spec: Two stacked panels, top and bottom, with a downward arrow between them. Top panel, green outline, numbered circle 1, titled 'Stack 1: create the cluster', containing one cluster icon box labelled google_container_cluster in monospace with the text 'Cluster provisioning'. The arrow between the panels carries the note 'The cluster must exist before this stack runs'. Bottom panel, numbered circle 2, titled 'Stack 2: configure the providers and add-ons', containing three boxes left to right connected by arrows: first a box with an arrow-in icon titled 'Data sources', text 'data google_container_cluster and data google_client_config'; second a box with a gear icon titled 'kubernetes and helm providers', text 'Configured from the data sources'; third a box with a puzzle icon titled 'Add-ons', text 'For example a GPU operator or an ingress controller'. Orange outline on the bottom panel title as the single most important rule: 'Build the cluster first, configure the providers in a later stack'. A green note to the left of the top panel: 'Provider endpoints are unknown at plan time when the cluster is created in the same apply.' Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Two stacks stop the cluster and its add-ons from failing together.'
anchor: ### Provider dependency ordering and the "provider depends on resource" problem
alt: Stack one creates the GKE cluster and stack two reads it with data sources to configure the kubernetes and helm providers.
cap: The cluster is created in one stack, and a second stack configures the Kubernetes and Helm providers from data sources.

name: a23-live-vs-modules
title: Reusable modules and deployable live stacks
spec: Two large side-by-side panels with a green heading each. Left panel titled 'modules/' with the note 'Reusable, versioned building blocks, nothing deploys by itself'. Inside it, four small blocks in a row labelled network, checkpoint-bucket, gke-cluster and gpu-pool, each with a box icon, and a fifth block iam-workload. Right panel titled 'live/' with the note 'Deployable stacks, one state each'. Inside it, a stack of three example boxes labelled prod, staging and lab (environment folders). Inside the prod box, a small grid of five stack boxes labelled network, storage, cluster, gpu-pools and observability, each with its own state icon (disk cylinder). A dashed arrow from the modules panel to the live panel, labelled 'Pinned version' in green, with the note 'Higher environments consume modules through pinned versions'. Orange outline on the stack box gpu-pools in prod, with the note 'A change here touches one pool in one region in production' as the single most important example. Numbered circles are not needed. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'A stack's path expresses its blast radius, so check the path first in a review.' Keep the dashed arrow as the only connector between panels.
alt: Reusable modules sit apart from live stacks, which are split by environment and region, each with its own state.
cap: Reusable modules live apart from the live stacks that deploy them, and each live stack path shows how far a change can reach.

name: a23-terragrunt-dry
title: One root file defines the backend for every stack below it
spec: Top: one wide box titled 'live/stage/terragrunt.hcl (root)', with the text 'remote_state defined once, with the key built from path_relative_to_include()' and a small key icon. Below it, a row of stack boxes connected from the root by downward arrows, each arrow labelled with the monospace text include { path = find_in_parent_folders() }. Child stack boxes: 'services/hello-world-app/terragrunt.hcl' (the state key shown as services/hello-world-app/terraform.tfstate) and 'data-stores/mysql/terragrunt.hcl'. Each child box shows its own state icon (disk cylinder) with its own key path, so each stack has its own state. A dependency arrow goes from the hello-world-app box to the mysql box, labelled with the monospace text dependency mysql { config_path = "../../data-stores/mysql" }, pointing at the mysql box. Number circles 1 to 3 beside the sequence of run: 1 'Run terragrunt run-all apply', 2 'Apply data-stores/mysql first', 3 'Then apply services/hello-world-app'. Orange outline on the root box as the single most important item: the backend is written only once. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Every stack gets its own state without anyone typing a key by hand.'
anchor: ### Keeping `live/` DRY with Terragrunt (*Terraform: Up and Running* Chapter 10)
alt: A root Terragrunt file defines the S3 backend once, child stacks include it, and run-all applies the mysql stack before the app stack.
cap: One root Terragrunt file defines the backend once, and each child stack gets its own state key from its folder path.

name: a23-test-stages
title: Skip the slow stages while you iterate
spec: A horizontal row of five stage boxes, left to right, each with a numbered circle (1 to 5, green) and a gear or test-tube icon, connected by arrows left to right. Stage 1 titled 'deploy_db' (monospace), with the note 'Slow, about 13 minutes'. Stage 2 titled 'deploy_app' (monospace). Stage 3 titled 'validate_app' (monospace). Stage 4 titled 'teardown_app' (monospace). Stage 5 titled 'teardown_db' (monospace). Below the row, a bracket spanning stage 1 and stage 5 labelled 'Skipped on later runs with SKIP_<stage>=true'. Under the bracket, a second line of monospace text: SKIP_deploy_db=true SKIP_teardown_db=true SKIP_teardown_app=true go test -timeout 30m. Above the stages, a green note: 'test_structure.RunTestStage wraps each stage, and the options are saved to disk'. Highlight stage 2 'deploy_app' and stage 3 'validate_app' in an orange outline as the stages that run on every iteration, the single most important part. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Keep the oven on between batches of cookies, rather than heating it from cold every time.'
alt: Test stages deploy_db through teardown_db, where skipping the database stages lets you iterate on the app stages alone.
cap: Splitting an integration test into named stages lets you skip the slow database stages and re-run only the application stages.

name: a24-private-egress
title: Private nodes reach Google and the internet without public IPs
spec: Centre: one large box titled 'GPU node' with a chip or server icon and the note 'No public IP', drawn with an orange outline as the single most important item. Left of the node: a box titled 'Private Google Access' with a cloud icon and the label 'Google APIs', connected to the node by an arrow pointing from the node to the box, labelled 'Outbound to Google APIs'. Below the node: a box titled 'Cloud NAT' with a router icon, connected by an arrow pointing from the node to the box, then a second arrow from Cloud NAT to a box titled 'Internet', labelled 'Outbound only'. Right of the node: a box titled 'Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)' with a lock icon and the small text '35.235.240.0/20', connected by an arrow pointing into the node, labelled 'gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap'. A blocked arrow from the Internet box pointing toward the node with a cross mark, labelled 'Nothing reaches the node inbound'. Above the node, a green note: 'Private Google Access lets a private VM call Google APIs, while Cloud NAT gives outbound-only internet access.' Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Outbound works through NAT, inbound SSH works through IAP, and no node needs a public address.' Use four arrows only, none crossing.
alt: A GPU node without a public IP reaches Google APIs through Private Google Access and the internet through Cloud NAT, and engineers SSH in through IAP.
cap: A GPU node with no public IP reaches Google APIs and the internet through private access and Cloud NAT, and engineers reach it through IAP.

name: a24-multi-nic
title: Multi-node GPU training with one VPC per GPU NIC
spec: Left: a tall box titled 'A3 GPU node' with a server icon, showing a row of GPU chips labelled GPU, with the text 'a3-highgpu-8g' underneath. From the right edge of this box, five network port icons. The top port is labelled 'Primary NIC' and connects by an arrow to a box at the upper right titled 'Management VPC', with the text 'General traffic' inside. The four lower ports, each labelled 'GPU NIC', each connect by an arrow to one of four stacked boxes at the lower right, each titled 'Extra VPC network' with the text 'mtu = 8896' and 'Own subnet'. Arrows from the four GPU NIC ports are labelled 'GPU-to-GPU traffic'. A bracket beside the four lower boxes is labelled 'Four or eight, one per GPU NIC', with an orange outline as the single most important item. A green note under the node: 'GPUDirect-TCPX, or GPUDirect-RDMA on A3 Ultra and A4'. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'The main NIC carries general traffic, while the extra NICs carry GPU-to-GPU traffic.' No arrows cross.
alt: One management VPC carries general traffic, and four or eight extra VPCs with mtu 8896 each carry GPU-to-GPU traffic from one GPU NIC.
cap: Multi-node GPU training adds one extra VPC per GPU NIC with jumbo MTU, while the primary NIC keeps general traffic.

name: a24-surge-upgrade
title: Why max_surge = 0 keeps a reserved pool upgradable
spec: Two side-by-side panels with a green heading each. Left panel titled 'Default surge: max_surge = 1, max_unavailable = 0'. Inside, a row of 16 small green GPU node boxes labelled as 'a3-highgpu-8g' nodes in a box titled 'Reservation: 16 nodes', all running. Beside them, one dashed extra node box in orange labelled 'Extra GPU VM' with an arrow pointing into the reservation box and a stop mark. Below, an outcome box with the text 'QUOTA_EXCEEDED or RESERVATION_EXHAUSTED' and the note 'The upgrade stalls'. Right panel titled 'max_surge = 0, max_unavailable = 1'. Inside, the same 16 nodes in the same reservation box, with one node highlighted and an arrow labelled 'Cordon, drain, upgrade one existing node at a time'. No extra node box. Outcome box in green with the text 'Stays inside the 16-node reservation'. Under both panels, a green note: 'A fixed reservation has no spare room for an extra node.' Number circles are not needed. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Upgrade one existing node at a time, so a reserved pool never needs capacity it does not have.'
anchor: ## 4. GKE clusters and GPU node pools
alt: A default surge upgrade needs a 17th GPU node that a 16-node reservation cannot hold, so max_surge 0 with max_unavailable 1 upgrades nodes in place.
cap: A surge upgrade needs an extra GPU node that a full reservation cannot hold, so max_surge 0 with max_unavailable 1 upgrades one existing node at a time.

name: a24-nebius-fabric
title: Create the fabric first, then attach every node to it
spec: Top: one wide box titled 'nebius_compute_v1_gpu_cluster' with a network or fabric icon, text 'InfiniBand fabric for multi-node NCCL', and the monospace label infiniband_fabric = "fabric-3". Number circle 1 beside it: 'Create the fabric first'. Below, a row of three instance boxes titled 'nebius_compute_v1_instance', each with a GPU chip icon and the monospace label gpu_cluster = { id = ... }, and the text 'one per node name'. Each instance box has an arrow pointing up to the fabric box, labelled 'refers to the fabric ID'. Three dots between the second and third instance boxes to show more nodes. Number circle 2 beside the instance row: 'Instances join the same fabric'. Orange outline on the arrows' label 'Every node in the same GPU cluster' as the single most important rule. A green note on the right: 'A node on the wrong fabric still runs, but it does not share fast links with its peers.' Green takeaway bar at the bottom: 'Place all the nodes of a training pool in one fabric, sized for the largest job you will run.'
alt: A Nebius GPU cluster creates the InfiniBand fabric first, and each instance refers to its ID so every node joins the same fabric.
cap: In Nebius, the GPU cluster fabric is created first, and every instance refers to its ID so all nodes share one InfiniBand fabric.

name: a25-two-stack-layering
title: Create the cluster in one state, configure providers in another
spec: Two horizontal rows, no time order, so no number circles. Top row, labelled Avoid, with a red-free layout in grey: a box with the text one state creates the cluster and configures the providers. An orange arrow from it labelled host unknown at plan time points to a box with the text provider falls back to the local kubeconfig and deploys into the wrong cluster. Bottom row, labelled Do, in green: a box labelled create the cluster in one state, then a green arrow labelled data sources read the cluster, pointing to a box labelled configure the kubernetes and helm providers in another state. The two boxes of the bottom row sit side by side inside a light green panel. Monospace labels for kubernetes and helm. No takeaway bar.
alt: Creating the cluster and configuring the providers in one state can deploy to the wrong cluster, so use two states with data sources.
cap: Put cluster creation and provider configuration in separate states, so the providers read the cluster through data sources.

name: a25-team-fanout
title: One team entry fans out into one copy of each resource per namespace
spec: Left: a box labelled team ml holding the namespaces dev and prod. An arrow labelled locals flatten points right to a light green container labelled local.ns (monospace) holding two keyed entries in monospace: ml-dev and ml-prod. A single arrow labelled one copy per entry leaves that container and points right to a larger container labelled for_each over each entry, holding four resource boxes stacked in monospace: kubernetes_namespace, kubernetes_resource_quota, kubernetes_role_binding, kubernetes_network_policy. Under the four boxes, a small note: add a third namespace and each resource gets one more copy. No takeaway bar.
alt: A team with dev and prod namespaces is flattened into two keys, and each resource is created once per key.
cap: One team with two namespaces flattens into two keys, and each tenancy resource is then created once per key.

name: a25-gitops-handoff
title: Terraform bootstraps Argo CD, then Git takes over
spec: Five boxes left to right with number circles 1 to 4 on the arrows or box corners, green. Box 1 labelled helm_release argocd (monospace), with a sub-label Terraform installs Argo CD. Arrow 2 to box labelled kubectl_manifest root_app (monospace), sub-label one Application called root. Arrow 3 to a box labelled Git folder clusters/cluster_name (monospace), sub-label the folder lists the rest of the cluster. Arrow 4 to a box labelled automated sync with prune and selfHeal (monospace), sub-label Git is the authority. Put the Terraform boxes 1 and 2 on a light green panel labelled Terraform bootstrap and the Git and sync boxes on a second panel labelled GitOps. Orange note under the GitOps panel: do not change anything Argo manages from Terraform. No takeaway bar.
alt: Terraform installs Argo CD and a root Application that points at a Git folder, then Argo CD keeps the cluster in sync.
cap: Terraform installs Argo CD and one root Application, and after that Git and Argo CD keep the cluster in sync.

name: a26-argo-status
title: Sync status and health status answer different questions
spec: Two cards side by side on a light green panel, no time order so no number circles. Each card has two status badges at the top: a badge labelled Sync status and a badge labelled Health status. Card 1 (left) shows badges Synced and Degraded (Synced in green, Degraded in grey). Under the badges, a short text: Git and the cluster agree, but the thing Git describes is broken, such as a GPU pod that cannot be scheduled. A footer line in the card: the fix is in the workload or its node pool. Card 2 (right) shows badges OutOfSync and Healthy. Text: something works, but it no longer matches Git, so a change was made somewhere it should not have been. Footer line: the fix is in whoever changed the object by hand. Above both cards, a single line showing the four health values in monospace: Healthy, Progressing, Degraded, Missing. Orange outline on card 2 only, as the most important warning. No takeaway bar.
alt: Synced with Degraded means Git and the cluster agree but the workload is broken; OutOfSync with Healthy means something was changed by hand.
cap: Sync status says whether the cluster matches Git, and health status says whether the workload actually works.

name: a26-flux-chain
title: Three Flux objects, each one feeding the next
spec: Three boxes in a row from left to right, with number circles 1, 2, 3 above them in green (time order: fetch, apply, install). Box 1 labelled GitRepository (monospace), with a sub-label fetches the files, and a small note inside it: polls Git every minute (interval 1m). Arrow from box 1 to box 2 labelled with the text files. Box 2 labelled Kustomization (monospace), sub-label applies some of them, with a note dependsOn crds keeps the CRDs ahead of the things that use them. Box 2 is the orange item, with an orange outline, because the dependsOn ordering is the key point. Arrow from box 2 to box 3 labelled with the text applies. Box 3 labelled HelmRelease (monospace), sub-label installs a chart, with a note: checks every half hour (interval 30m). Each box has a simple icon: a folder for GitRepository, a gear for Kustomization, a package for HelmRelease. Light green panel behind the three boxes. No takeaway bar.
alt: A Flux GitRepository fetches files, a Kustomization applies them after its dependsOn, and a HelmRelease installs a chart.
cap: In Flux, a GitRepository fetches the files, a Kustomization applies them, and a HelmRelease installs the chart.

name: a26-repo-layout
title: One cluster directory points at shared infrastructure and app overlays
spec: Left column: a large light green container labelled clusters/ (monospace) with a sub-label one directory per cluster: what runs there. Also inside the container, a smaller box labelled staging-eu (monospace) with no arrows. Right column, top: a container labelled infrastructure/ (monospace) with sub-label platform components shared by clusters, holding a box base/ listing gpu-operator, network-operator, cert-manager, ingress, monitoring, kueue, policies (monospace, wrapped on several lines) and a box overlays/ listing staging and prod (monospace). Right column, bottom: a container labelled apps/ (monospace) with sub-label tenant and team applications, holding base/ listing inference-gateway and training-pipelines, and overlays/ listing staging and prod. Orange outline on the clusters/ container as the root of reconciliation. No takeaway bar.
alt: A cluster directory holds an infrastructure and an apps file, each pointing at the prod overlay of its shared folder.
cap: Each cluster directory says what runs there, and it points at the prod overlays in the shared infrastructure and apps folders.

name: a27-play-order
title: Four site.yml plays run in order, each one a stage with a gate
spec: Four boxes in a row from left to right, joined by three arrows, with green number circles 1, 2, 3, 4 at the top of the boxes (time order). Box 1 titled Base for every node, sub-label hosts: all, role base_os in monospace. Box 2 titled GPU nodes, sub-label hosts: gpu, and inside it three monospace lines: serial: 34% then 100%, max_fail_percentage: 0, roles gpu_stub or nvidia_driver then node_validate. Inside box 2, a small first-batch sub-box labelled gpu01 (canary) and a second sub-box labelled gpu02 and gpu03. Orange outline on the max_fail_percentage: 0 line as the gate: one failure stops everything else. Box 3 titled Controller services, sub-label hosts: controller, roles monitoring and munge_slurm. Box 4 titled Workers join the scheduler, sub-label hosts: gpu, role munge_slurm, then a post task node_validate. Each box has a simple icon: a server rack for base, a chip for GPU nodes, a gear for controller services, a window or plug for the workers. Light green panel behind the four boxes. No takeaway bar.
anchor: ### 2.3 Site playbook with ordering and safety
alt: The site playbook configures base nodes, then GPU workers in a canary batch, then the controller, then joins the workers to the scheduler.
cap: The site playbook runs four plays in order, and the GPU play starts with one canary node that can stop the rollout.

name: a27-path-contract
title: Path A and Path B sit behind one module contract
spec: Top: a box labelled var.nodes (monospace) with a sub-label role and gpus per host. Two arrows leave it, one to the left module and one to the right module. Middle row, two side-by-side boxes. Left box titled Path A: nodes_docker, sub-label systemd and sshd containers on 172.28.0.0/24, ports 2200 plus i. Right box titled Path B: nodes_gcp, sub-label VPC, Cloud NAT, IAP firewall, service account and VMs. Both boxes have one arrow pointing down into one shared box below them titled output nodes (monospace), with the fields role, gpus, address, ssh_host, ssh_port listed as lines inside it. Then one arrow from that box down to a box titled generated hosts.yml (monospace), then one arrow right to a box titled ansible site.yml, sub-label unchanged on both paths. A small orange tag on the Ansible box reading gpu_tools_stub: true on Path A and false on Path B, marked as the only switch. Light green panel behind the shared output and Ansible part. No takeaway bar.
alt: Two backends take the same node map and return the same output, so the Ansible playbook runs unchanged.
cap: Path A and Path B return the same node output, so the Ansible playbook runs unchanged and only the GPU tools switch changes.

name: a27-pipeline-stages
title: The pipeline: a cheap static job, then plan-and-test, then destroy always
spec: Left to right, three job columns, with a green arrow between each pair. Above the left column, a small label line: pull_request and nightly schedule 30 3 * * * (monospace), with no arrow. Column 1, titled static (monospace) with sub-label cheap, fails fast: four stacked step boxes in monospace or plain text: terraform fmt check, terraform validate, yamllint and ansible-lint, gitleaks. Arrow labelled needs: static (monospace) to Column 2, titled plan-and-test with sub-label expensive: step boxes in order: Apply ephemeral lab, Configure and verify with site.yml run, a second site.yml run with changed=0 gate (orange outline on this box as the idempotency gate), then verify.yml. Arrow labelled if: always() (monospace) to Column 3, a single box titled Destroy (always) with sub-label terraform destroy runs no matter what happened above it. Light green panel behind each column. No takeaway bar.
alt: The static job checks format, lint and secrets, plan-and-test applies and verifies the lab, and destroy always runs at the end.
cap: The pipeline runs cheap static checks first, then the apply and verify job, and always destroys the lab at the end.
